clue.text: Piano directly behind you — this type?

parts.note: the text-message spelling of the word
p is the mark in a score for playing softly
right behind you is directly behind you

explanation.surface: A piano standing immediately at your back, and a question about which kind it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This type?' points two ways at once: the answer is the piano that stands on end, and it is also the plain roman type this clue is printed in, as opposed to italic.
explanation.definitionFit: this type? -> UPRIGHT: the piano built tall rather than long, and equally the unslanted type the clue itself is set in.

clue.text: Topless beefcake welcoming keen response to get at the drink?

indicators.note: in a down entry the top of a word is where it starts, so a topless one has lost its first letter
to welcome someone is to take them inside, so the letters named next sit within this piece

parts.note: a beefcake is a HUNK, and down the column its top letter comes away
'Cor!' is the British noise of eager admiration

explanation.surface: A shirtless muscleman lapping up an admiring gasp before heading for the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is a picture rather than a synonym: the drink is behind the cork, and this is the move that reaches it.
explanation.definitionFit: get at the drink? -> UNCORK: pulling the cork is the one thing standing between a bottle of wine and the person wanting a glass.

clue.text: Wine bringing hint of shakiness into part of eye

indicators.note: the barest hint of a word is the letter it opens with, all you get before the rest arrives

parts.note: the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eyeball

indicators.note: what goes into something ends up inside it, so this letter is planted within the other piece

parts.note: the letter this word opens with, taken as the indicator asks

explanation.surface: A wine that puts the first tremor into the drinker's eye.
explanation.walkthrough: Retsina is the Greek white flavoured with pine resin, which is why setters reach for it whenever a wine is wanted. The eye part is the one crosswords use most often.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine -> RETSINA: one particular bottle standing for the general word, the resinated white drunk all over Greece.

clue.text: Roman poet, half-cut, gambles on hard legendary king

indicators.note: cut in half, with the surface's tipsiness as the joke; the word keeps only half its letters, and it is the back half that joins on here

parts.note: VIRGIL, who wrote the Aeneid, keeps only his second half
to game is to gamble, so the gambles are games
the H stamped on a hard pencil

explanation.surface: A tipsy Roman poet having a flutter on something difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British for tipsy, which is what makes the surface work while the instruction just wants half the letters. Gilgamesh rules Uruk in the Babylonian epic, the oldest story we have.
explanation.definitionFit: legendary king -> GILGAMESH: the king of Uruk in the Mesopotamian epic, a monarch known only from legend.

clue.text: Edward supporting name adopted by present family, being sensitive

indicators.note: a family that adopts takes somebody into itself, so this letter is planted inside the piece named next
in a down entry whatever supports the rest holds it up from underneath, so this piece takes the bottom squares

parts.note: the present one is this one
n. is the short form on any form asking for one
your kin are your family
Ned is the old pet form of Edward, as Ted is

explanation.surface: Edward standing behind the name the present generation of the family has taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' is the adjective here, not a gift and not a verb, which is the trap the surface sets. Ned for Edward is worth banking alongside Ted and Ted's own Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: sensitive -> THIN-SKINNED: skin too thin to keep a slight out, the standard idiom for anyone quick to take offence.

clue.text: Remains with company after start of critical week? It's a profitable business

indicators.note: what comes after something is written to its right in an across entry, so the two pieces named first follow the letter named next
the start of a word is the letter it begins with

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
what remains after a fire is ash
Co. as in Smith & Co.
w is the diary's short form for week, and the question mark flags the shorthand

explanation.surface: What is left of a firm at the beginning of a difficult week.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'start of critical week?' as one phrase. Only the first word is trimmed; the week hands over its own abbreviation whole.
explanation.definitionFit: a profitable business -> CASH COW: the product or firm you keep milking for steady money, from the cow that never stops giving.

clue.text: Family disposing of large container

indicators.note: to dispose of something is to get rid of it, so the letter named next is thrown out of the word before it

parts.note: a clan is a family, the Scottish sense
L is the size on a clothing label — the letter the family loses

explanation.surface: A household getting rid of an outsized container.
explanation.walkthrough: Clan for family is the one to bank here: Scottish, and a crossword regular. The container of the definition is a tin, not the thing being dragged to the tip.
explanation.definitionFit: container -> CAN: the tin a drink or a tin of soup comes in, a container in the plainest sense of the word.

clue.text: Organisation that's leading in tennis?

definitions.note: The second definition describes a scoreline rather than offering a synonym: a player who has won one more set than the opponent is said to be a set up, and the question mark is the setter admitting the stretch.
definitions.meaning: the way an outfit is arranged and run, the whole apparatus of it
tennis is scored in sets, and the player one of them ahead of the other is the one in front

explanation.surface: An organisation that leads the field in the world of tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading' is the hinge: pre-eminent in the surface, ahead on the scoreboard in the wordplay. Nothing here is being built out of letters, which is why the enumeration's hyphen is the only clue to the shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Organisation -> SET-UP: the arrangement an outfit is run on; and on court a player a set ahead of the other is a set up.

clue.text: Legendary creature's heart mostly filled with gold

indicators.note: mostly the word but not all of it, so the final letter is left off
what is filled has something put inside it, so this piece opens up to take the letters named next

parts.note: the heart of a thing is its CENTRE, which gives up its last letter here
Au is gold on the periodic table, from the Latin aurum

explanation.surface: Some creature out of myth with a core of gold in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart' usually tells a solver to take the middle letters of a neighbouring word; here it wants the word CENTRE itself. Centaurs are the horse-bodied men of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Legendary creature -> CENTAUR: the half-man, half-horse of Greek myth, a beast that exists only in stories.

clue.text: Question about weird tale by English horror writer

indicators.note: to go about something is to go round it, so this piece wraps itself round the letters named next
something weird is out of its natural order, so these letters will not be staying in theirs

parts.note: the question word itself, spelt out
the four letters of TALE with the E of English joined on, shuffled

explanation.surface: A query raised about a strange story from an English writer of horror.
explanation.walkthrough: Dennis Wheatley sold millions of black-magic thrillers in the mid-twentieth century, The Devil Rides Out among them. 'Question' is the word WHY rather than a synonym for query.
explanation.definitionFit: horror writer -> WHEATLEY: Dennis Wheatley, the British novelist whose occult thrillers made him the best-selling name in the genre in his day.

clue.text: Lively dance giving you time in twist with hero

indicators.note: a letter put in something goes inside it, so this one lands between the letters of the piece named next

parts.note: a twist of rope or wire is a coil
t is the standard short form, as on a timetable
a lion of a man is a hero; Richard the Lionheart is the same idea

explanation.surface: A brisk dance in which you spend some time whirling round with a hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist' looks like another dance and is a coil of rope instead. The cotillion is the eighteenth-century ballroom dance for four couples that the quadrille grew out of.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively dance -> COTILLION: the quick eighteenth-century ballroom dance for four couples, and in America still the name for a formal ball.

clue.text: Painting evidently involves a touch of colour

indicators.note: what a thing involves is carried inside it, so the letters are already sitting in these words rather than being built out of them

parts.note: five letters running consecutively out of the middle of the first word and into the second

explanation.surface: A painting that plainly has a little colour about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place is the good kind: painting and colour belong to the same picture, so nothing in the sentence looks like a lid over anything.
explanation.definitionFit: a touch of colour -> TINGE: a tinge is a trace of colour rather than a coat of it, exactly the small amount the definition allows.

clue.text: Blokes getting out of clothing, meeting a dish from India

indicators.note: the blokes climb out of the clothing, so those letters are taken out of the word that was holding them

parts.note: clothing is RAIMENT, and three letters walk out of the middle of it
the clue's own letter, taken as it stands
blokes are men — the three letters that leave

explanation.surface: Blokes climbing out of their clothes and sitting down to an Indian meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Raiment is the old word for clothing, and it is where the blokes have to be found before they can be got out of. The side dish itself is yoghurt with cucumber or mint.
explanation.definitionFit: dish from India -> RAITA: the yoghurt side dish, usually with cucumber or mint, served alongside a curry to cool the heat.

clue.text: Chap's not at liberty to accept unknown supplier of sugar or butter

indicators.note: letters at liberty are free to go wherever they like, so they will not be staying in the order given
to accept something is to take it in, so the extra letter joins the others before they are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
x, y and z are algebra's unknowns

explanation.surface: A man under some restriction, not free to take on a mystery something.
explanation.walkthrough: The split is the whole trick: 'not' belongs with the letters being shuffled, and 'at liberty' is the instruction, so the surface's sense of confinement is the opposite of what the words are doing.
explanation.definitionFit: supplier of sugar or butter -> SYCOPHANT: the flatterer who sugars his words and butters people up, both idioms for laying it on thick.

clue.text: Historic works surrounding small office of medical specialist

indicators.note: to work dough or clay is to knead it out of shape, and these letters get the same treatment
what surrounds a thing closes round it on both sides, so the shuffled letters go either side of the piece named next

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
a pod is the small self-contained workspace an open-plan floor is divided into

explanation.surface: Old industrial works standing round a small office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' reads as a factory in the surface and as the instruction to knead in the wordplay, which is where the whole clue turns. The shuffled letters land either side of the office.
explanation.definitionFit: medical specialist -> CHIROPODIST: the foot specialist, trained on one part of the body rather than practising generally.

clue.text: Target of pilgrimage in rocky Spain etc if not entirely gone astray?

indicators.note: a rocky surface is uneven and unsettled, so these letters will not stay standing in the order given
not entirely the word, so the last letter of it is left off

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
to have gone astray is to have ERRED, and the last letter of that is dropped

explanation.surface: A pilgrim's goal somewhere in rugged Spain, if it has not been entirely lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Etc' and 'if' are letters here, not connectives, which is what makes the fodder so hard to see. Cape Finisterre is the Galician headland the Romans took for the end of the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Target of pilgrimage -> CAPE FINISTERRE: the Atlantic headland many walkers on the Camino press on to after Santiago, finishing at the sea.

clue.text: Fisherman's info? Start of tall fish story involving bass

indicators.note: a story that involves something has it inside, so this letter goes within the piece named next
the start of a word is the letter it begins with

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
the ide is a freshwater fish of the carp family and a crossword regular
a story is a tale
b is the musical shorthand for the bass part

explanation.surface: The opening of a tall fishing story with a bass somewhere in it.
explanation.walkthrough: A tall story is an exaggeration, which is what makes 'tall fish story' read as one phrase when only the first word is being used. The ide is a real fish, not a made-up one.
explanation.definitionFit: Fisherman’s info? -> TIDE TABLE: the printed times of high and low water, which is what anyone working a boat off the coast plans the day around.

clue.text: Son's preparing potatoes? Excellent

definitions.note: The answer ends in -ing but is an adjective rather than a participle here, so a plain adjective defines it: a smashing holiday is an excellent one.

parts.note: s. is the short form used in a family firm's name
one way of preparing potatoes, and the question mark admits it is only one of several

explanation.surface: A son at the stove doing the potatoes, and doing them well.
explanation.walkthrough: The British use of the answer as a term of delight is the point — nothing in this clue gets broken. The question mark is there because mashing is only one thing you can do to a potato.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent -> SMASHING: the everyday British term of approval, as in a smashing time, with no breakage involved.

clue.text: Instructions to leave militant religious groups?

parts.note: militants are the ones out on the streets, on the march
an order is a community of monks or nuns, and the question mark flags that it is one kind of religious group among many

explanation.surface: Advice on how to get out of a militant religious sect.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting your marching orders is being dismissed — told to go, in the army and out of it. Read the surface way, the clue offers a route out of a cult.
explanation.definitionFit: Instructions to leave -> MARCHING ORDERS: what you are given when you are sacked or sent packing, the army's phrase for being moved on.

clue.text: Unrestrained, like Brazil-NY flight?

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro standing in for the country it sits in
a flight runs from one place to another, and the hyphen in the clue is that 'to'
New York is in the United States, so the city stands for the country

explanation.surface: An airline route out of Brazil to New York, described as wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Timetables write a route with a dash where speech says 'to', and that dash is the middle of the answer. The word keeps its party sense here rather than its rioting one.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrestrained -> RIOTOUS: riotous laughter or a riotous night out is the unrestrained kind, with nobody actually rioting.

clue.text: Dance with repeated element? Sweet

parts.note: the Cuban ballroom dance
the two letters the dance ends on, said a second time

explanation.surface: A dance built round a step that keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: The element repeated is a syllable of the dance, not a step in it, which is what the question mark is warning about. A rum baba is the small yeast cake drenched in rum syrup.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet -> RUM BABA: in Britain the sweet is the pudding course, and this soaked yeast cake is one of its old standards.

clue.text: Positive cry for help, being short of money? When will money arrive?

definitions.note: The definition is put as a question rather than as a synonym: the answer is what you would say in reply, naming the day the money comes rather than glossing a word.

indicators.note: m is the shorthand for money in a set of accounts, and a word short of money gives up exactly that letter

parts.note: P marks the positive terminal on a battery
the radio distress call, from the French m'aidez, help me, which arrives here one letter lighter

explanation.surface: An upbeat distress call from somebody who has run out of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayday comes from the French m'aidez, help me, which is why the call sounds nothing like a plea in English. 'Positive' is the battery terminal's P, one of the quieter conventions.
explanation.definitionFit: When will money arrive? -> PAYDAY: the day the wages land in the account, which is the answer anyone short of cash is waiting to hear.

clue.text: Cartoon character's news story curtailed by having opening trimmed

indicators.note: to curtail is to dock the tail, so the word gives up the letter it ends with
a trimmed hedge has had its outermost growth cut away, and this word loses its last letter the same way

parts.note: a news story got in ahead of the rivals is a SCOOP, docked here of its final letter
the word is used for its own two letters
an opening in a wall is a DOOR, with the end cut off

explanation.surface: A news story cut short, with its opening paragraph trimmed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks like the usual instruction to take a first letter, and here it is a doorway. Scooby-Doo is the cowardly Great Dane of the Hanna-Barbera cartoons.
explanation.definitionFit: Cartoon character -> SCOOBY-DOO: the talking Great Dane who solves mysteries with a gang of teenagers in the cartoon series named after him.

clue.text: In US, marshy spot in inlet not wholly dismissed

indicators.note: not the whole of the word, so its last letter is left behind

parts.note: a bay is an inlet of the sea
a batter dismissed is OUT, and the word does not arrive whole

explanation.surface: A swampy American spot in a bay, not entirely written off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dismissed' is the cricket scoreboard's out, the umpire's verdict on a batter. Bayous are the slow, weed-choked creeks of Louisiana and the delta country.
explanation.definitionFit: In US, marshy spot -> BAYOU: the sluggish, swampy creek of the Mississippi delta, a word used in the American South and nowhere else.

clue.text: You shouldn't have to go round some current American city

indicators.note: going round something means passing either side of it, so this piece closes round the letters named next

parts.note: the British thank-you, the thing you say over a present
the amp is the unit electric current is measured in, so some of it is an amp

explanation.surface: A polite protest at being made to drive round an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have' is a thank-you in disguise, the phrase said over a gift rather than an objection to anything. 'Current' is the electrical one, not the present-day one.
explanation.definitionFit: American city -> TAMPA: the port on Florida's Gulf coast, one of the largest cities in the state.

clue.text: Soldiers probing climber for key material

indicators.note: a probe goes into the thing it is examining, so these letters are pushed inside the piece named next

parts.note: ivy is the climbing plant on the wall
OR is Other Ranks, the British army's term for everyone below officer

explanation.surface: Troops going through a mountaineer's things in search of vital evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: OR for soldiers is one of the conventions worth learning early, and the climber is a plant rather than a person. The key of the definition is the piano's.
explanation.definitionFit: key material -> IVORY: what piano keys were cut from before plastic, which is why pianists still talk about tickling the ivories.

clue.text: Good rate given to directors for stationery item

parts.note: to go at a good clip is to go at a fair rate
a company's directors sit together as its board

explanation.surface: A favourable rate offered to a company's directors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At a good clip' is the phrase behind the first half, meaning speed rather than money. Directors and board is the pairing crosswords use more than any other.
explanation.definitionFit: stationery item -> CLIPBOARD: the stiff board with a spring clip along the top, sold beside the pads and folders.

clue.text: Encouragement to speak with charm, wasting time

indicators.note: what is wasted is lost, so the letter named next disappears from the word before it

parts.note: something charming is cute
t is the standard abbreviation — the letter that goes to waste

explanation.surface: Winning somebody over with charm while the clock runs down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charm' is the adjective cute, not a bracelet's charm, and that swap of part of speech is the difficulty in three letters. The answer is the actor's signal that the next line is theirs.
explanation.definitionFit: Encouragement to speak -> CUE: the signal an actor waits for before delivering a line, and by extension any prompt to start talking.

clue.text: Indicate end of these tracks, say, turning back

indicators.note: turning back means reading the other way, and across the grid that is right to left, all three pieces at once
the end of a word is the letter it finishes on

parts.note: the last letter of the word, taken as the indicator asks
the tracks a wheel leaves in soft ground are ruts
e.g. is the Latin shorthand for 'say' or 'for example'

explanation.surface: A note pointing at where this set of tracks stops and doubles back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning back' governs everything named before it rather than the nearest word alone, so all seven letters turn together. 'Say' is the two letters of e.g., a workhorse worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Indicate -> GESTURE: to gesture towards something is to indicate it with a hand or a nod rather than with words.

clue.text: Charge accepted by those people providing form of treatment

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so these letters go inside the piece named next

parts.note: those people are they
a rap is a criminal charge — to take the rap is to take the blame for it

explanation.surface: A fee that certain people are willing to accept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' is the police one rather than the fee the surface offers, and taking the rap is the phrase behind it. Nobody in this clue is being paid anything.
explanation.definitionFit: form of treatment -> THERAPY: treatment by means other than drugs or surgery — talking, exercise, heat — each of which is a therapy.
